memory_candidates.content: When a teammate reports 'you appear idle' based on stale artifact mtimes while you are actually mid-diagnosis on a slow background reproduction loop (e.g. 8x sequential ~3-minute verify-deploy.sh runs), send an immediate SendMessage status update with concrete partial findings rather than waiting silently for the loop to finish. Silence during a genuinely long-running diagnostic reads identically to having done nothing, from the outside -- there is no way for a caller to distinguish 'actively working on a slow task' from 'stalled' without an explicit interim signal. Checkpoint the reasoning and partial evidence gathered so far to a message (or to disk) well before the full loop completes, especially when a session context-clear is a live possibility.

When a shell-based CI/lint gate internally re-invokes a full test suite runner as a captured command substitution ($(...)), `ps`/`pstree` can show the intermediate subshell with the SAME argv as its parent script (e.g. a gate script appearing to recursively re-invoke itself), because bash's fork-for-command-substitution does not always rewrite argv before exec'ing the final command. This is a normal, benign artifact of process-tree inspection, not evidence of accidental recursion -- verify by checking whether the 'child' process's own children match the expected real invocation (e.g. the actual test-runner script) before concluding there is a recursion bug.

A test suite that drives a REAL backgrounded process (e.g. `sleep 300 &`, killed and then polled with `kill -0` to confirm death before asserting liveness-check semantics) is inherently load-sensitive: under a fuller concurrent suite run, PID reap/zombie-cleanup can take longer than an isolated run, producing an intermittent failure correlated with system load rather than with any defect in the code under test. If such a suite's own comments already document a prior widening of its polling budget for exactly this reason, treat that as a strong signal that further intermittent failures in a heavier-load context (e.g. inside a CI gate that re-runs the full suite alongside dozens of others) are very likely the SAME pre-existing load-sensitivity, not a new defect -- before assuming an unrelated recent change (e.g. a concurrency fix in a completely different subsystem) is the cause.
